env_header:
catena: client-editable, non-secret configuration.

GENERATED from catena-ce/ansible/helpers/knobs.yml. To change a key or its
explanation, edit that file and run `python3 helpers/render_knobs.py
--write`; an edit made here is replaced by the next render, and fails the
CI check until then.

Copy it to `.env` inside a host directory (gitignored), one per inventory
so several hosts coexist in one checkout: inventory/example/.env,
inventory/clientco/.env. Ansible resolves <inventory_dir>/.env through the
`dotenv` lookup plugin at playbooks/lookup_plugins/, and group_vars reads a
value with "{{ lookup('dotenv', 'KEY') }}".

No secret belongs in here, or anywhere else in an inventory. Every secret
lives on the target at /etc/catena/config.json, minted there or entered in
catena-admin > Settings. See catena-ce/SECRETS.md.

gui_steps.name: target
gui_steps.title: The server
gui_steps.doc:
Where Catena is going, and the key that reaches it. A machine that
already exists: the launcher does not order one, because ordering means
holding a client's cloud credentials.
gui_steps.validates:
The address answers on the SSH port, and the keypair is on this machine
(the launcher offers to generate one when it is not).

gui_steps.name: domain
gui_steps.title: The domain
gui_steps.doc:
The name this server answers on. Every address it publishes is a name
under it, and the token is what lets the server create them.

Blank is a real answer. A server installed with no domain finishes with
no public surface and is reached over the private network; the domain and
its token are entered together in the panel afterwards, and the next
converge publishes it.
gui_steps.validates:
The token is live, it reaches this domain, and the domain is ACTIVE at
Cloudflare. A domain still waiting on its registrar's nameservers
resolves nowhere, so an install on one would publish records nobody can
follow.

gui_steps.name: access
gui_steps.title: Getting back in
gui_steps.doc:
How this server is reached for maintenance after the install. On the
private network the installer closes the public SSH port once it has
proven the new path from this machine; without one the port stays open,
because a server with no other way in has nothing to prove.
gui_steps.validates:
The credential exchanges for a token at the provider, and this machine
can reach the network it joins. Both, because minting a key for a network
this machine cannot reach produces a server nobody here can administer.

gui_steps.name: backup
gui_steps.title: Backup
gui_steps.doc:
Where snapshots go. The repository is ONE address that already carries
the endpoint and the bucket, and the keys are what open it.

This is also the keyset a client keeps: with the repository, the two S3
keys and the restic password, a wiped server is rebuilt from nothing
else.
gui_steps.validates:
The endpoint answers. Whether the credentials open the repository is
proven by the first backup, on the server, where restic runs.

gui_steps.name: locale
gui_steps.title: Language and time
gui_steps.doc:
The server's own locale and timezone. They decide what its logs and its
scheduled jobs are stamped with, not what the panel is read in -- the
panel switches language per visitor.
gui_steps.validates: Nothing to prove: both are settings on the server itself.

gui_steps.name: keyset
gui_steps.title: Save these
gui_steps.doc:
The passwords the server mints for itself and shows ONCE: the first-login
password, the backup encryption password, and the console break-glass
password. Nothing off the server holds a copy.
gui_steps.validates:
An explicit acknowledgement that they are saved. This step is the last
one and it cannot be skipped: without it the launcher ships installs
nobody can recover.

env_sections.name: host
env_sections.title: Host
env_sections.doc:
Where the box is and how the first SSH lands on it, before the ops
account exists and before the firewall closes.

env_sections.name: ssh
env_sections.title: SSH
env_sections.doc:
Generate the pair once:

    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/catena_ed25519 -C catena

env_sections.name: access
env_sections.title: Access
env_sections.doc:
How this host is reached for administration. Two methods, and the choice
decides whether public port 22 can be closed at all.

`tailnet` joins a private network before anything else is reachable, and
the install closes public 22 once it has PROVEN the tailnet path from
the machine that is about to lose it. `public_ssh` joins no network and
keeps 22 open, because a host with no alternative path has nothing to
prove and closing it would be a lockout.

The keys below SEED the on-box store on the first converge and are never
read again. After the install the choice lives in catena-admin >
Settings > Access and tunnels, which is where a client changes it;
editing them here afterwards changes nothing.

On the tailnet method there are two providers. Tailscale SaaS: leave
TAILNET_PROVIDER blank or set it to `tailscale`, and `catena install`
prints the one-time admin-console steps, then prompts for the OAuth
client id and secret. Headscale: set TAILNET_PROVIDER=headscale and fill
the two below it; `catena install` prompts instead for a
headscale_api_key (preferred, a short-lived tagged pre-auth key is
minted per run) or a static headscale_preauth_key.

Either credential is asked for at install rather than in the panel,
because it is what JOINS the host to the tailnet and the panel is
published on that tailnet. Rotating it later is a Settings job;
supplying it the first time cannot be.

env_sections.name: cloudflare
env_sections.title: Cloudflare
env_sections.doc:
Filling the domain in makes `catena install` ask for the API token that
publishes it, and the tunnel comes up during the install. Leaving it
blank installs a server with no public surface; the domain and the token
are then entered together in catena-admin > Settings, and the next
converge publishes it.

env_sections.name: storage
env_sections.title: Storage
env_sections.doc:
App data and the Docker data-root live under one prefix on the disk this
host already has: /srv/catena, which the backup set, the volume layout
and the restore machine all name. Catena does not manage block devices.
More space is a disk the client mounts themselves, bind-mounts into the
app, and declares in backup_extra_paths so the backup set knows about it.

env_sections.name: development
env_sections.title: Development only
env_sections.doc:
Leave every key in this section at its default on a client install.
They point certificate issuance at a local Pebble or at Let's Encrypt
staging, whose certificates browsers, TURN clients and sending MTAs all
reject. The test bench sets them to its own host-side ACME server.

secrets.doc: The one credential the public surface needs. The account id is not an input: the host engine resolves it from the token.
Multi-domain (Business): a JSON map of zone to API token, each token scoped to its one zone. The panel's domains page owns it, so it is not a field on the settings form.

Tailscale SaaS mints a per-converge tagged auth key from this client, so nothing long-lived lands on the VPS. Required on that path, hidden on the Headscale one, so the badge is only read where it is true.

Headscale has no OAuth API. The node joins with a pre-auth key, minted per converge from this one (preferred, nothing long-lived on the VPS). Either this or the static key satisfies the converge, so neither is required on its own.
The static fallback when no API key is stored. Long-lived, hence second.
The one mail credential, whichever provider is chosen: the Resend API key, the Brevo SMTP key, or the relay's password.
Configures the mailserver APPLICATION, not the host's shared outbound path, so it belongs to that template's own configuration rather than the mail group on the settings page.
The mailserver template's Spamhaus subscription. Same reasoning.

CIFS credentials for the optional bulk mount. Client-held: the share is the client's NAS. NFS authenticates by source IP and supplies neither. The storage role's bulk.yml names both on the settings page when it asks for them, so the page has to offer them under exactly these names.

A signed claim rather than a shared secret: this repo neither mints nor verifies it, it only stores it. Optional -- Community is the default and an empty field must stay empty rather than reading as "not set yet".
The optional client portal's billing keys. Never minted; billing routes degrade gracefully while they are blank.

config.doc: The provider's public IPv4. Used during bootstrap, before the firewall closes and the box is reached another way.
The provider's default login for that same phase (root, ubuntu, debian, ec2-user). Not OPS_USER -- that account does not exist yet.
The port the controller CONNECTS on, written into hosts.yml as ansible_port. The firewall rules name 22 literally, so a value here moves what the controller dials and not what the host opens.
A dedicated keypair for this project, so revoking at engagement end is throwing away one file. The installer offers to generate it when absent.

The non-root account created on every VPS, authorized for the key above. A variable and not a question: it defaults to `ops`, every host uses that, and it is named in sshd's AllowUsers, the sudoers drop-in, the home paths and the bootstrap probes -- so the launcher does not ask, and an operator who needs a different one sets it in the inventory.

Comma-separated tags advertised by each node. Every tag must be authorized on the control server first, or key minting rejects with a 400. Read with NO default, so a missing key fails the lookup rather than falling back to a tag the credential is not scoped for.
Whether Tailscale may override systemd-resolved. Usually false.
A separate optional tier over CIFS or NFS, independent of the primary disk. Append-only data only: never database storage, never the Docker data-root.

THE identity of the install: every public hostname is <sub>.<zone>, so this is the value the rest of the page renders against. Blank is a real state -- a server is installed before its domain is decided, and the public surface defers until one arrives.

One address for the Portainer admin and the initial realm admin. The matching password is minted on the box and shown once at the end of the install, with the first-login URLs. A host fact by any reading, which is why the `.env` only seeds it.

The one subdomain three sources give three answers for -- `portainer` in the shipped starter, `apps` in the operator skeleton, `admin` for established clients -- which is what makes it a host fact rather than the product's. The rest are the product's scheme and are compiled in, because a host has to converge itself without reading this file.

Prefixes the name of the tunnel a host creates. Blank leaves each host owning one tunnel named after its inventory hostname; a prefix of "corp-" on a host named "vps1" names the tunnel "corp-vps1". A store key because the host composes its own tunnel name and reads the prefix straight off the store, which is what lets the cloudflared actions ship in the image instead of being rendered by a converge.

How this host is reached for administration, and therefore whether public port 22 can be closed. `tailnet` closes it once the tailnet path has been proven from the machine about to lose it; `public_ssh` keeps it open, because a host with no alternative path has nothing to prove and closing it would be a lockout. A stored value rather than a derived one: it rides /etc into the snapshot, so a rebuilt host comes back with the firewall posture it had rather than the one a default would pick.

Which control plane the tailnet runs on. Blank means Tailscale SaaS. Explicit rather than inferred from whether a control URL happens to be filled in: that inference made "switch back to Tailscale" mean "know to CLEAR a field", and a blank submission on the settings page means "leave this alone", so the client could make that decision in one direction only.
The Headscale server's base URL.
The Headscale user the minted pre-auth keys belong to; Headscale keys are per-user, and the advertised tag must be in THAT user's tagOwners.

Absolute paths outside /srv/catena to include in the backup, separated by commas. This is what a client who mounted their own disk declares: the product carves its prefix out of the disk the host already has and does not manage block devices, so a bind mount from somewhere else is invisible to the backup set until it is named here. The nightly coverage lane reads the same value, so one declaration both captures the path and stops it reading as an uncovered bind-mount source.

Lengthens the effective cadence beyond the base timer. No Ansible projection: the backup wrapper reads it off the store at runtime, with no converge in between. There is deliberately no enable switch beside it -- whether a host backs up is answered by whether the endpoint is usable and whether the lane is scheduled, and a third answer could disagree with both.

The offsite-copy lane's dead-man endpoints. WHICH buckets it copies is not a knob: that is the store's offsite_copies list, read straight off disk so adding a copy takes effect with no converge in between.
`none` is a real stored value, not a blank: a blank submission means "leave this alone", so an off position spelled as the empty string would be a control that could turn mail on and never off.

ONE address, whichever provider routes it. A field per provider (RESEND_SENDER_EMAIL, BREVO_SENDER_EMAIL, SMTP_FROM, one non-empty at a time) would make the converge infer which is active, and switching provider would mean knowing to CLEAR the old field rather than filling the new one -- leaving it filled would keep sending through the provider the client just left.
Applies to the `server` choice only.
The `server` relay's login, and also the Brevo one, which is account-specific unlike Resend's.
Must be hard to guess -- anyone who knows it can post to it.

Whether every account must enrol a second factor. A choice rather than free text because the converge renders it straight into the realm's required-action config, where a value it cannot read as a boolean would either fail the import or silently mean off. The identity probe reads the resulting posture back and reports drift, which is the pair this completes.
Optional apt HTTP proxy, typically an apt-cacher-ng. Blank pulls direct. HTTPS sources stay direct either way. A site policy rather than an install input.
Optional pull-through mirror, as a base URL with scheme, host and port. Blank pulls from docker.io directly.
Issue the coturn TLS-TURN certificate from Let's Encrypt's staging CA. Staging has no rate limit and coturn only validates presence and expiry.
The same, for the self-hosted mailserver's mail.<zone> certificate.
A local ACME server's directory endpoint. Blank issues against Let's Encrypt as normal.
Mapped to the hostname `pebble` in /etc/hosts, Pebble's endpoint-cert SAN.
Base64 because a raw multi-line PEM cannot live in a `.env`.
